```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

Most tools of control engineering work on linear models. A nonlinear model
\[
x' = f(x, u, p, t), \qquad y = h(x, u, p, t)
\]
with inputs \(u\) and outputs \(y\) is approximated near an operating
point \((x_0, u_0)\) by the linear state space model
\[
\delta x' = A\, \delta x + B\, \delta u, \qquad \delta y = C\, \delta x + D\, \delta u,
\]
with the Jacobians \(A = \partial f / \partial x\), \(B = \partial f /
\partial u\), \(C = \partial h / \partial x\) and \(D = \partial h /
\partial u\). modelcompR computes these matrices from the symbolic model,
as ModelingToolkit's `linearize` does, and supports the analysis points
of ModelingToolkit for the sensitivity functions of feedback loops. This
article covers

* `linearize()` with named inputs and outputs and operating points,
* symbolic linearization, linearization functions and problems,
* differential algebraic models,
* using the state space matrices in base R: poles, frequency responses
  and step responses,
* analysis points, sensitivity functions and loop transfer functions of a
  feedback loop built from components,
* opening loops, and generating control functions.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(modelcompR))
t <- t_nounits
D <- D_nounits
```

## Linearizing a model

A damped pendulum driven by a torque \(\tau\) has the angle \(\theta\) as
its measured output. Inputs and outputs are marked with the `input` and
`output` metadata of their variables, like `[input = true]` in Julia.

```{r}
theta <- Variable("theta", t)
omega <- Variable("omega", t)
tau <- Variable("tau", t, input = TRUE)
angle <- Variable("angle", t, output = TRUE)
g <- Parameter("g", default = 9.81)
len <- Parameter("len", default = 1)
b <- Parameter("b", default = 0.5)
pend <- System(list(D(theta) ~ omega,
                    D(omega) ~ -g / len * sin(theta) - b * omega + tau,
                    angle ~ theta), t, name = "pend")
```

`linearize(sys, inputs, outputs, op = ...)` takes the unsimplified model.
It compiles the model with the inputs kept as external signals, solves for
a consistent operating point and evaluates the Jacobians there. The result
holds the four matrices, the names of the `states` (the order of the
unknowns of the simplified system), the simplified system `sys` and the
operating point used, `extras`.

```{r}
down <- linearize(pend, list(tau), list(angle), op = list(theta ~ 0, omega ~ 0, tau ~ 0))
down$states
down[c("A", "B", "C", "D")]
```

The operating point is a list of equations `variable ~ value`; parameters
not given take their defaults, and `p` gives further parameter values.
Linearizing at the upright position gives an unstable model: one
eigenvalue of \(A\) is positive.

```{r}
up <- linearize(pend, list(tau), list(angle), op = list(theta ~ pi, omega ~ 0, tau ~ 0))
up$A
eigen(down$A)$values
eigen(up$A)$values
```

A different damping is passed with `p`:

```{r}
linearize(pend, list(tau), list(angle), op = list(theta ~ 0, omega ~ 0, tau ~ 0),
          p = list(b ~ 2))$A
```

### Symbolic linearization

`linearize_symbolic()` returns the same matrices as symbolic expressions,
along with the Jacobian blocks it is built from. It shows how the
linearization depends on the operating point and the parameters.

```{r}
sym <- linearize_symbolic(pend, list(tau), list(angle))
sym$A
sym$B
```

## Operating points and repeated linearization

Each call of `linearize()` compiles the model. When the same model is
linearized at many operating points, the compiled form can be reused.

### Linearization functions

`linearization_function(sys, inputs, outputs, op)` (ModelingToolkit's
`linearization_function`) compiles once and returns `lin_fun`, a function
of the numeric state, parameters and time that returns the Jacobian
blocks, and the simplified system `sys`. `linearize(ssys, lin_fun, op =
...)` then linearizes without compiling again.

```{r}
lf <- linearization_function(pend, list(tau), list(angle),
                             op = list(theta ~ 0, omega ~ 0, tau ~ 0))
lf$lin_fun
linearize(lf$sys, lf$lin_fun, op = list(theta ~ 1))$A
```

The blocks follow the semi-explicit form \(x' = f(x, z, u)\), \(0 = g(x,
z, u)\), \(y = h(x, z, u)\), where \(z\) are algebraic unknowns:

```{r}
unknowns(lf$sys)
parameters(lf$sys)
blocks <- lf$lin_fun(c(0.5, 0), c(1, 9.81, 0.5, 0), 0)
names(blocks)
blocks$f_x
blocks$f_u
```

The numeric vectors are ordered as `unknowns(lf$sys)` and
`parameters(lf$sys)`; the input \(\tau\) has become the last parameter of
the compiled system.

### Linearization problems

`LinearizationProblem()` wraps a linearization function with a mutable
operating point. Values are set with `prob[x] <- value`, and `solve()`
linearizes at the current point; this mirrors `LinearizationProblem` and
`setu`/`setp` in Julia.

```{r}
lp <- LinearizationProblem(pend, list(tau), list(angle),
                           op = list(theta ~ 0, omega ~ 0, tau ~ 0))
lp
angles <- seq(0, pi, length.out = 5)
vapply(angles, function(a) {
  lp[theta] <- a
  solve(lp)$A[2, 1]
}, 0)
```

The entry \(A_{21} = -(g / \ell) \cos\theta\) changes sign at
\(\theta = \pi / 2\), where gravity stops pulling the pendulum back.

### Operating points along a trajectory

`LinearizationOpPoint(sol, t)` takes the operating point from a
simulation. With several times, `linearize()` returns one linearization
per time, which is how gain scheduled controllers are designed.

```{r}
sim <- ODEProblem(mtkcompile(pend, inputs = list(tau)),
                  list(theta ~ 2, omega ~ 0, tau ~ 0), c(0, 5))
psol <- solve(sim, Tsit5())
along <- linearize(pend, list(tau), list(angle), op = LinearizationOpPoint(psol, c(0, 2.5, 5)))
vapply(along, function(l) l$A[2, 1], 0)
-9.81 * cos(psol(c(0, 2.5, 5))[, 1])
```

## Algebraic unknowns

For a model with algebraic equations, the state of ModelingToolkit's
linearization contains all unknowns of the simplified system,
\((x, z)\), and
\(A = \begin{pmatrix} f_x & f_z \\ G f_x & G f_z \end{pmatrix}\) with
\(G = -g_z^{-1} g_x\). With `eliminate_algebraic = TRUE` the algebraic
unknowns are eliminated through the implicit function theorem,
\(z = -g_z^{-1}(g_x x + g_u u)\), which gives the minimal state. In the
example below \(z\) cannot be solved for symbolically, so it stays an
unknown after compilation.

```{r}
w <- Variable("w", t)
z <- Variable("z", t, guess = 1)
v_in <- Variable("v_in", t, input = TRUE)
dae <- System(list(D(w) ~ -w + z + v_in, 0 ~ z^3 + z - w), t, name = "dae")
full <- linearize(dae, list(v_in), list(w), op = list(w ~ 2, v_in ~ 0))
full$states
full$A
reduced <- linearize(dae, list(v_in), list(w), op = list(w ~ 2, v_in ~ 0),
                     eliminate_algebraic = TRUE)
reduced$A
```

At \(w = 2\) the constraint gives \(z = 1\), and \(dz/dw = 1 / (3 z^2 + 1)
= 1/4\), so the reduced model has \(A = -1 + 1/4 = -3/4\).

## Using the state space matrices

The matrices are plain R matrices, so base R covers the usual analyses.

### Poles and stability

The eigenvalues of \(A\) are the poles of the linear model. The hanging
pendulum has a lightly damped pair with natural frequency
\(\sqrt{g / \ell}\) and damping ratio \(b / (2 \sqrt{g / \ell})\):

```{r}
ev <- eigen(down$A)$values
c(natural_frequency = Mod(ev[1]), damping_ratio = -Re(ev[1]) / Mod(ev[1]))
c(sqrt(9.81), 0.5 / (2 * sqrt(9.81)))
```

### Frequency response

The transfer function \(G(s) = C (sI - A)^{-1} B + D\) is evaluated at
\(s = i \omega\) with `solve()`:

```{r}
freqresp <- function(lin, w) {
  vapply(w, function(wi) {
    as.complex(lin$C %*% solve(1i * wi * diag(nrow(lin$A)) - lin$A, lin$B) + lin$D)
  }, 0i)
}
wgrid <- 10^seq(-1, 2, length.out = 300)
G <- freqresp(down, wgrid)
plot(wgrid, 20 * log10(Mod(G)), log = "x", type = "l", xlab = "frequency (rad/s)",
     ylab = "magnitude (dB)", main = "Pendulum torque to angle")
abline(v = sqrt(9.81), lty = 3)
```

The resonance peak sits at the natural frequency.

### Step response

For a stable \(A\), the response to a unit step in the input from the
operating point is \(\delta x(t) = A^{-1}(e^{At} - I) B\). The matrix
exponential follows from the eigendecomposition \(A = V \Lambda V^{-1}\)
when \(A\) is diagonalizable:

```{r}
expm_eigen <- function(A, s) {
  e <- eigen(A)
  Re(e$vectors %*% diag(exp(e$values * s), nrow(A)) %*% solve(e$vectors))
}
step_response <- function(lin, times) {
  vapply(times, function(s) {
    x <- solve(lin$A, (expm_eigen(lin$A, s) - diag(nrow(lin$A))) %*% lin$B)
    as.numeric(lin$C %*% x + lin$D)
  }, 0)
}
tt <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)
plot(tt, step_response(down, tt), type = "l", xlab = "t", ylab = "angle",
     main = "Unit torque step")
abline(h = -down$C %*% solve(down$A, down$B), lty = 3)
```

The response settles at the static gain \(-C A^{-1} B = \ell / g\).

### Changing coordinates

`similarity_transform(lin, T)` changes the state coordinates with
\(x = T x_2\), and `reorder_unknowns(lin, old, new)` permutes the states.
The poles do not change:

```{r}
Tm <- matrix(c(1, 1, 0, 1), 2)
tr <- similarity_transform(down, Tm)
tr$A
eigen(tr$A)$values
reorder_unknowns(down, down$states, rev(down$states))$A
```

## A feedback loop from components

Control systems are usually assembled from blocks connected through
signal connectors, as in the ModelingToolkitStandardLibrary. The blocks
below are defined with `connector()` and `mtkmodel()`, the counterparts of
`@connector` and `@mtkmodel`: a first order plant \(P(s) = k / (T s + 1)\),
a PI controller \(C(s) = k_p + k_i / s\), and an error block \(e = r - y\)
with the reference \(r\) as a parameter.

```{r}
RealInput <- connector("RealInput", variables = list(list("u(t)", input = TRUE)))
RealOutput <- connector("RealOutput", variables = list(list("u(t)", output = TRUE)))
SISO <- mtkmodel("SISO", variables = list("u(t)", "y(t)"),
  components = list(input = quote(RealInput()), output = quote(RealOutput())),
  equations = quote(list(u ~ input$u, y ~ output$u)))
FirstOrder <- mtkmodel("FirstOrder", extend = list(siso = quote(SISO())),
  parameters = list("T = 1", "k = 1"), variables = list("x(t) = 0"),
  equations = quote(list(D(x) ~ (k * u - x) / T, y ~ x)))
PI <- mtkmodel("PI", extend = list(siso = quote(SISO())),
  parameters = list("kp = 1", "ki = 1"), variables = list("xi(t) = 0"),
  equations = quote(list(D(xi) ~ u, y ~ kp * u + ki * xi)))
ErrorBlock <- mtkmodel("ErrorBlock", parameters = list("r = 0"),
  components = list(input = quote(RealInput()), output = quote(RealOutput())),
  equations = quote(list(output$u ~ r - input$u)))
```

### Analysis points

An analysis point is a named connection: `connect(out, "name", in)`
creates an `AnalysisPoint` that behaves like an ordinary connection in
simulation, and marks the signal for linear analysis. It is referred to as
`sys$name` on the unsimplified model. Here every connection of the loop is
an analysis point: `y` (the measurement), `e` (the error) and `u` (the
control signal).

```{r}
P <- FirstOrder(name = "P", k = 2, T = 0.5)
C <- PI(name = "C", kp = 1, ki = 2)
E <- ErrorBlock(name = "E")
loop <- System(list(connect(P$output, "y", E$input),
                    connect(E$output, "e", C$input),
                    connect(C$output, "u", P$input)),
               t, systems = list(P, C, E), name = "loop")
loop$u
```

The PI zero at \(-k_i / k_p = -2\) cancels the plant pole at \(-1 / T =
-2\), so the loop transfer function is \(P C = 4 / s\) and the closed loop
from reference to output is \(4 / (s + 4)\). A simulation of a unit
reference step confirms it:

```{r}
cl_sys <- mtkcompile(loop)
cl_prob <- ODEProblem(cl_sys, list(E$r ~ 1), c(0, 2))
cl_sol <- solve(cl_prob, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8, saveat = 0.5)
rbind(simulated = cl_sol[P$y], exact = 1 - exp(-4 * cl_sol$t))
```

### Sensitivity functions

The classical loop functions at a point of the loop are

* the sensitivity function \(S = 1 / (1 + PC)\), the transfer from a
  disturbance added at the point to the signal there,
* the complementary sensitivity function \(T = PC / (1 + PC) = 1 - S\),
* the loop transfer function \(L\), the response around the opened loop.

`get_sensitivity(sys, ap)`, `get_comp_sensitivity(sys, ap)` and
`get_looptransfer(sys, ap)` linearize them at the analysis point `ap`, as
in ModelingToolkit; they return the same structure as `linearize()`.

```{r}
S <- get_sensitivity(loop, loop$u, verbose = FALSE)
Tc <- get_comp_sensitivity(loop, loop$u, verbose = FALSE)
L <- get_looptransfer(loop, loop$u, verbose = FALSE)
S[c("A", "B", "C", "D")]
```

The state space realizations keep the cancelled plant pole, so the
eigenvalues of `S$A` are \(-4\) and \(-2\); the transfer functions
themselves are \(S = s / (s + 4)\), \(T = 4 / (s + 4)\) and, with the
negative feedback sign that ModelingToolkit includes, \(L = -4 / s\).
Evaluating them on the imaginary axis checks this and the identity
\(S + T = 1\):

```{r}
s_test <- c(0.5, 2, 10)
rbind(S = freqresp(S, s_test), S_exact = 1i * s_test / (1i * s_test + 4),
      T = freqresp(Tc, s_test), L = freqresp(L, s_test), L_exact = -4 / (1i * s_test))
max(Mod(freqresp(S, wgrid) + freqresp(Tc, wgrid) - 1))
```

The peak of \(|S|\) is a standard robustness measure: its inverse is the
distance from the Nyquist curve to the critical point. For this loop
\(|S|\) rises monotonically toward 1 at high frequency and never exceeds
it, the best possible value.

```{r}
Sw <- freqresp(S, wgrid)
Tw <- freqresp(Tc, wgrid)
plot(wgrid, 20 * log10(Mod(Sw)), log = "x", type = "l", ylim = c(-40, 5),
     xlab = "frequency (rad/s)", ylab = "magnitude (dB)")
lines(wgrid, 20 * log10(Mod(Tw)), lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("S", "T"), lty = 1:2, bty = "n")
max(Mod(Sw))
```

Several analysis points at once give a multivariable function:

```{r}
get_sensitivity(loop, list(loop$u, loop$y), verbose = FALSE)$D
```

`get_sensitivity_function()`, `get_comp_sensitivity_function()` and
`get_looptransfer_function()` return the linearization function and the
simplified system instead, for repeated linearization:

```{r}
Sf <- get_sensitivity_function(loop, loop$u, verbose = FALSE)
Sf$lin_fun
```

### Linearizing between analysis points

Analysis points can be used as the inputs and outputs of `linearize()`.
An input point adds a perturbation to its signal, an output point reads
the signal. From the error point to the measurement point the transfer is
the complementary sensitivity, which is also the reference to output
response:

```{r}
ry <- linearize(loop, loop$e, loop$y, verbose = FALSE)
ry[c("A", "B", "C", "D")]
step_response(ry, c(0.25, 0.5, 1))
1 - exp(-4 * c(0.25, 0.5, 1))
```

### Opening loops

`loop_openings` breaks connections before linearizing. Opening the loop at
the measurement and linearizing from the control signal to the
measurement gives the plant alone, \(P(s) = 4 / (s + 2)\), together with
the controller state that no longer affects the output:

```{r}
plant <- linearize(loop, loop$u, loop$y, loop_openings = list(loop$y), verbose = FALSE)
plant[c("A", "B", "C", "D")]
freqresp(plant, 1)
4 / (1i + 2)
```

`open_loop(sys, ap)` performs the same transformation on the model and
returns it, together with `du`, the new input that now drives the
destinations of the point, and `u`, the variable that drove it:

```{r}
ol <- open_loop(loop, loop$y)
ol$du
ol$u
ol_lin <- linearize(ol$sys, ol$du, list(ol$u), verbose = FALSE)
freqresp(ol_lin, 1)
```

The transfer from the measurement input of the error block back to the
plant output is \(-PC = -4 / s\), the loop transfer function at \(y\).

`linearization_ap_transform()` exposes the transformation that
`linearize()` applies to analysis point inputs and outputs, adding the
perturbation variables:

```{r}
tr_ap <- linearization_ap_transform(loop, loop$u, list(), list())
tr_ap$inputs
```

### Hierarchical models

Analysis points of subsystems are reached through the hierarchy, and their
names are namespaced like any other variable:

```{r}
plant_room <- System(list(), t, systems = list(loop), name = "room")
room_ap <- plant_room$loop$u
room_ap
get_sensitivity(plant_room, room_ap, verbose = FALSE)$D
```

A string name of the point, relative to the model, works as well:
`get_sensitivity(plant_room, "loop₊u")`.

## Control functions

`generate_control_function(sys, inputs)` compiles a model with the given
inputs and returns the function \(f(x, u, p, t)\) of \(x' = f(x, u, p,
t)\), the unknowns `dvs` and parameters `ps` that order its arguments,
and the compiled input output system `io_sys`. It is the starting point
for model predictive control and state estimation, where the dynamics are
evaluated directly.

```{r}
cf <- generate_control_function(pend, list(tau))
cf$dvs
cf$ps
pvals <- unname(c(len = 1, g = 9.81, b = 0.5)[vapply(cf$ps, format, "")])
cf$f(c(0.1, 0), 0.2, pvals, 0)
```

`calculate_control_jacobian()` gives the symbolic Jacobian of the dynamics
with respect to the inputs, and `unbound_inputs()` lists inputs that no
equation drives:

```{r}
calculate_control_jacobian(cf$io_sys)
unbound_inputs(pend)
```

## Summary

| Task | modelcompR | ModelingToolkit |
|:--|:--|:--|
| linearize at an operating point | `linearize(sys, inputs, outputs, op = )` | `linearize` |
| symbolic matrices | `linearize_symbolic()` | `linearize_symbolic` |
| reuse the compiled model | `linearization_function()`, `LinearizationProblem()` | the same |
| operating points from a simulation | `LinearizationOpPoint()` | the same |
| analysis points | `connect(out, "name", in)`, `AnalysisPoint()` | `connect(out, :name, in)` |
| loop functions | `get_sensitivity()`, `get_comp_sensitivity()`, `get_looptransfer()` | the same |
| open a loop | `loop_openings = `, `open_loop()` | the same |
| coordinates | `similarity_transform()`, `reorder_unknowns()` | the same |
| dynamics for control | `generate_control_function()` | the same |
